claims.text: The studied material is a Co-free, equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-crystal FCC solid solution.
Dislocation nucleation initiates at vacancy clusters or disordered atomic regions.
Plastic flow is mediated predominantly by Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vectors of the 1/6<112> type.
Shockley partial motion creates intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults.
Stacking-fault formation produces localized HCP-like regions without a complete bulk phase transformation.
Yielding is marked by a sudden stress drop associated with dislocation nucleation at vacancy sites.
Increasing temperature enhances thermal vibrations and lowers the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation nucleation.
The thermally assisted reduction in nucleation stress causes yield strength to decrease as temperature increases from 10 K to 600 K.
Higher strain rates impede dislocation annihilation or recovery.
Dislocation density increases as strain rate increases from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength is negligibly sensitive to strain-rate changes between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
Loading along the <-111> direction gives a higher yield strength than loading along <110> or <1-12>.
The maximum yield strength under <-111> loading results from its resolved shear stress for partial-dislocation slip.
Deformation in the tested regime occurs through localized stacking faults rather than a bulk FCC-to-BCC transformation.
Deformation in the predicted loading direction occurs without twinning.
The hypothesis applies only to single-crystal FCC FeNiCrMn between 10 K and 600 K and strain rates of 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.

Stress-strain curves, DXA dislocation densities, and CNA structural classifications can distinguish the predicted nucleation and stacking-fault mechanism across the controlled temperature, strain-rate, and orientation comparisons.
